deep.reconstruction:
Context: E598 is Euler's response to Lagrange's 'Recherches d'arithmétique' (1773-75). Euler classifies all primes p that divide some number p²+39q², i.e. primes with (-39/p)=1, according to their residue mod 4n=156.

On the previous page Euler enumerated the reduced forms of determinant -39 (discriminant -156): x²+39y², 3x²+13y² and 5x²±2xy+8y². This gives three 'classes' of prime divisors D:
- class I: D=F, where F = p²+39q²;
- class II: 3D=F;
- class III: 5D=F.
He takes the 24 reduced residues a<78 coprime to 156 and must attach to each a sign: +a if primes ≡a (mod 156) are divisors, -a if primes ≡ -a are. He also attaches the class.

How the signs are obtained:
- Squares give class I.
- p=1: 1+39=40 shows 5 is a +, class III divisor. Multiplying class I residues by 5 gives class III.
- p=4: 16+39=55 shows 11 is a + divisor of class III.

On this page:
- Class I residues {+1,+25,+49,-35,-23,+61} times 11 give the class III residues +11,-37,+71,-73,+59,+47.
- Class III residues {+5,+41,-31,-19,-67,-7} times 11 give class I residues +55,-17,-29,-53,+43,-77. This uses the product rule I·III=III, III·III=I.
- All 24 residues are now signed, and none falls in class II. So class II merges with class I.

The reason is that 3r²+13s² represents the square 16 (r=s=1). Hence D in class II has 16D = 3·16D... more precisely D·16 is of form p²+39q², so D = (p/4)²+39(q/4)² rationally. Example: 61=(25/4)²+39(3/4)², while integrally 61=3·4²+13·1² and 3·61=183=12²+39.

The negative residues are converted to complements mod 156. Euler then lists the primes up to 312 that are divisors. Corollary 1 (§44) proves the general composition identity
(fr²+2grs+hs²)(ft²+2gtu+hu²) = (frt+g(ts+ru)+hsu)² + n(ts−ru)², with fh−g²=n.
So the product of two values of the same form is a value of the principal form. If one factor can be a square (k=3+13=16), the class reduces to the principal one by admitting fractions.

In modern terms: h(-156)=4 with cyclic class group Z/4. There are two genera:
- principal genus {x²+39y², 3x²+13y²}: p≡1 (mod 3) and (p/13)=1;
- other genus {5x²±2xy+8y²}: p≡2 (mod 3) and (p/13)=−1.
Euler's 'classes' I and III are exactly the genera, recognized via rational (fractional) representability. The completeness claim (every such prime is a divisor) rests on quadratic reciprocity, still unproved at the time.
errors: The list of positive residues contains 113 where 103 is meant. 103 = 156−53 is the complement of the residue −53, and 103 = 8²+39·1². 113 is not a divisor: (−39/113) = −1, since 113≡2 (mod 3). The class mark 'I' printed under it fits 103, confirming a misprint.
Consequently the list of prime divisors below 312 wrongly contains 113 and omits 103.
The same list also wrongly contains 269 (=113+156). Here (−39/269) = (3/269)(13/269) = −1·1 = −1, so 269 divides no number p²+39q². No prime should replace it, because 103+156=259=7·37.
In the signed table the residue 35 is printed without its sign. It must be −35, as given by 11² ≡ −35 (mod 156) on the previous page and by the complement 121 in the later list.
All other signs and class marks I/III check against the genus characters (p mod 3, p mod 13). The multiplications by 11 and the composition identity in §44 are correct.

ideas.what: Classification of prime divisors of p²+39q² by residues mod 156, with signs ±a, using multiplicativity of classes (I·III=III, III·III=I).
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic character (−39/p) as a Dirichlet character mod 156; genus characters
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Tomus XIV observations, 1744/1751), Lagrange 1775, Legendre, Gauss (genus theory, 1801)
ideas.where_published: E164 'Theoremata circa divisores numerorum in hac forma pa²±qb² contentorum' (Comment. Acad. Petrop. 14), and E598 itself

ideas.what: Class 3D=F merges with class D=F because 3r²+13s² represents the square 16, giving a representation with denominator 4 (61=(25/4)²+39(3/4)²).
ideas.modern_name: Genus = rational equivalence class of forms (forms in the same genus are equivalent over Q with controlled denominators)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones (genus theory); Minkowski/Hasse for the rational-equivalence formulation
ideas.where_published: E598 (this paper); Euler's late papers on divisors of quadratic forms, discussed in Weil's 'Number Theory: An approach through history'

ideas.modern_name: Composition of a form with itself lands in the principal class (duplication / class of f² principal for ambiguous-type use); a special case of Gauss composition

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine worked example (n=39) in a well-known paper responding to Lagrange. The 'class II collapses into class I' phenomenon is Euler's pre-Gaussian glimpse of genera as rational classes, which is already discussed in the historical literature (e.g. Weil). The only new items are uncorrected misprints/errors: 113 for 103, the spurious 269, and the missing sign on 35.
transcription_corrections: Residue '35' in the first signed row should read '−35' (the sign is missing in print as well).
The second positive-residue list prints 113; the mathematically correct value is 103. This is a printing error, not a transcription error.
Character rows match the image: first list 'I III III I III I III I I III I III I III III I' and second 'III I III I I III I III'.
